## Why This Is Asked
Examines ability to design practical, team-wide guardrails at Namespace and Pod levels using policy engines in a real CI flow. Tests understanding of Kubernetes primitives (ResourceQuota, LimitRange, resources, securityContext) and how to surface failures early.

## Key Concepts
- ResourceQuota
- LimitRange
- Pod resource requests/limits
- SecurityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem)
- Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper integration
- Local and CI validation patterns

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal Kyverno policy skeletons (illustrative)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: require-namespace-quota-limitrange
spec:
  rules:
  - name: quota-in-namespace
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Namespace"]
    validate:
      message: "Namespace must declare ResourceQuota and LimitRange"
      pattern: {}
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest sketch (missing quotas/limits)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: example/app:latest
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt policies for existing namespaces with no quotas?
- What metrics would you surface to measure policy effectiveness?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical expertise in multi-tenant security, using real-world tools (cosign, Rekor, Kyverno, KMS) to enforce image provenance at CI time. It emphasizes tenant isolation, key management, and concrete verification steps.

## Key Concepts
- Cosign-based image signing with per-tenant keys stored in a central KMS
- Rekor-backed provenance verification
- Kyverno policy enforcing signatures and digest pinning across repos
- CI gating via GitHub Actions, plus local verification workflow

## Code Example
```yaml
# GitHub Actions gate (high level)
name: Image Signatures Gate
on: pull_request
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Install cosign
        run: curl -fsSL https://toolkit.cosign.is/cosign-linux-amd64 -o /usr/local/bin/cosign && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/cosign
      - name: Fetch tenant key from KMS
        run: |
          echo "Fetching tenant key..." # placeholder
      - name: Verify images in manifests
        run: |
          cosign verify --key <tenant-key> image digest
```
```yaml
# Kyverno policy snippet (digest-signature & tag checks)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-cosign-signature
spec:
  rules:
  - name: image-signature
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: [Deployment, Job, KnativeService]
    validate:
      message: "Image must be cosign-signed with tenant key"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - image: ?*
              - imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you rotate tenant keys without downtime?
- How would you audit failures and respond to a signature mismatch in production?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to express policy-as-code for security/compliance in multi-cloud clusters, combining network isolation, identity controls, and outbound security.

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper/OPA ConstraintTemplate
- NetworkPolicy as runtime guard
- Pod securityContext and automountServiceAccountToken control
- mTLS and central CA validation for outbound traffic
- CI verification using kubectl, gatekeeper audits

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8snetworkidentity
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sNetworkIdentityConstraint
  targets:
  - target: Kubernetes
    rego: |
      package k8snetworkidentity
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind == "Deployment"
        not has_ns_deny_ingress(input)
        msg := "Deployment namespace must have a deny-ingress NetworkPolicy and allow only whitelisted sources."
      }
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest (no deny ingress and automount enabled)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: example-fail
  namespace: dev
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: example-fail
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: example-fail
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest (deny ingress, trusted SA, automount disabled)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-sa
  namespace: dev
  annotations:
    trusted.example.io: "true"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: example-pass
  namespace: dev
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: example-pass
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: example-pass
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: app-sa
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

```yaml
# Minimal NetworkPolicy (deny ingress by default, allow from trusted namespace)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-ingress
  namespace: dev
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          env: trusted
```

## CI Verification Steps
- Gatekeeper audit run in CI to ensure constraints are evaluated.
- kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f failing.yaml should trigger policy violations.
- kubectl apply -f passing.yaml should succeed and Gatekeeper should record no violations.
- Validate that namespaces have the required NetworkPolicy objects and that deployments use trusted SAs with automountServiceAccountToken disabled.

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked

Tests practical, auditable governance for multi-team clusters beyond image/security gates.

Key Concepts

- Namespace governance with ResourceQuota and LimitRange
- Namespace-scoped RBAC and ServiceAccounts
- Lightweight CI gates using kubectl/yq
- Local validation vs CI parity

Code Example

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
  kubectl -n "$ns" get resourcequota >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing ResourceQuota in $ns"; exit 1; }
  kubectl -n "$ns" get limitrange >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing LimitRange in $ns"; exit 1; }
  for dep in $(kubectl -n "$ns" get deploy -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {/end}'); do
    sa=$(kubectl -n "$ns" get deploy "$dep" -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName}')
    if [ -z "$sa" ]; then echo "Deployment $dep in $ns uses default SA"; exit 1; fi
    kubectl -n "$ns" get rolebinding | grep -q "$sa" || { echo "Missing RBAC for $sa in $ns"; exit 1; }
  done
done
```

Failing manifest

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      name: app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
```

Passing manifest

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.memory: 16Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: lr
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - max:
      cpu: "4"
      memory: 8Gi
    min:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: sa-team-a
  namespace: team-a
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: sa-team-a-view
  namespace: team-a
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: sa-team-a
  namespace: team-a
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      name: app
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: sa-team-a
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:1.21
```

Verification

- Locally: run the gate script against your cluster context and verify it fails/passes as expected; inspect output for missing quota/limitrange or RBAC gaps.
- CI: run the same script in a workflow step; ensure failing manifests fail the build and passing manifests pass.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical enforcement of runtime posture using admission controls and network egress in a multi-tenant data platform. Combines Gatekeeper and Kyverno with real-world constraints.

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate with REGO to require envoy-proxy sidecar in confidential pods
- Kyverno policy enforcing non-root, readOnlyRootFilesystem and sidecar presence
- NetworkPolicy egress allowlist for data exfiltration guardrails
- CI test plan with manifest validation; runtime validation via in-cluster policy, egress monitoring

## Code Example
```rego
package k8svalidation

deny["envoy-proxy sidecar required"] {
  input.review.object.metadata.labels["data-tier"] == "confidential"
  not has_sidecar(input.review.object.spec.containers, "envoy-proxy")
}

has_sidecar(containers, name) {
  containers[i].name == name
}
```

```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: confidential-pod-security
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: require-envoy-sidecar
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              data-tier: confidential
    validate:
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: envoy-proxy
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of simple security defaults in Kubernetes and CI gates that prevent risky deployments.

## Key Concepts
- NetworkPolicy basics: default-deny, ingress/egress rules
- CI gate that scans manifests across namespaces
- Local + CI validation workflow

## Code Example
```yaml
# .github/workflows/netpol-gate.yml
name: NetPol Gate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  netpol-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          version: 'latest'
      - run: kubectl version --client
      - run: |
          for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
            kubectl -n $ns get networkpolicy >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing NP in $ns"; exit 1; }
          done
```

```yaml
# examples/fail/no-netpol.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: example
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
```

```yaml
# examples/pass/default-deny.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress: []
  egress: []
```

- How would you extend this gate to auto-create the default-deny NP if missing?
- How would you adapt for namespaces created by a gateway or CI namespace isolation?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests integration of policy-as-code, attestation, and runtime security across a multi-tenant cluster. Candidates must show how to bind OPA, Kyverno, Rekor/cosign, and Falco to a coherent workflow, plus a concrete verification plan.

## Key Concepts

- Image provenance and attestations (cosign, Rekor)
- Policy-as-code (OPA, Kyverno)
- Runtime security (Falco/eBPF)
- Multi-tenant governance and testability

## Code Example

```javascript
// OPA Rego (conceptual)
package kubernetes.admission
violation[reason] {
  input.review.object.kind == "Pod"
  image := input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image
  not imageIsAttested(image)
  reason = "image provenance missing"
}
```

```javascript
// Kyverno policy (conceptual)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-provenance-and-security
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: require-nonroot
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "must set runAsNonRoot and readOnlyRootFilesystem"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              runAsNonRoot: true
  - name: require-attested-image
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "image must have Rekor cosign attestation"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - image: "*attested*"
```

```javascript
// Falco rule (conceptual)
- rule: Unsigned Image Usage
  condition: container.image.signature == ""
  output: "Unsigned image detected: %container.image.repository"
  priority: WARN
```

- How would you handle attestation key rotation?
- How would you measure false positives and performance impact?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests end-to-end security design for multi-cloud Kubernetes workloads, focusing on identity, secret management, and policy enforcement with real-world tools.

## Key Concepts
- Zero-trust workload identity (SPIRE)
- Ephemeral credentials (Vault)
- Service mesh security (Istio, mTLS, AuthorizationPolicies)
- Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego)
- Egress controls to data lake and namespace isolation

## Sample Solution

### 1. SPIRE Workload Identity
```yaml
# spire-workload.yaml
apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterSPIFFEID
metadata:
  name: data-platform-workload
spec:
  names:
    - data-service
    - analytics-service
    - etl-service
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production
```

### 2. Vault Integration for Secrets
```yaml
# vault-secret-store.yaml
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultSecret
metadata:
  name: data-lake-credentials
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  vaultAddress: https://vault.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:8200
  path: secret/data-lake
  provider: hcp
  refreshInterval: 1h
```

### 3. Istio AuthorizationPolicy
```yaml
# istio-authz.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: data-lake-access
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: data-lake-gateway
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["spiffe://data-platform/data-service"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
        paths: ["/v1/tables/*"]
```

### 4. OPA Policy Example
```rego
#.rego
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.namespace == "restricted"
  not input.request.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg = "Pods must run as non-root"
}

allow[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment"
  input.request.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged
  msg = "Privileged containers not allowed"
}
```

### 5. CI Enforcement Check
```yaml

# ConstraintTemplate (RBACWhitelist)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:

spec:
```

## Why This Is Asked

This checks practical CI gating for namespace discipline and Helm workflow. It exercises a concrete validation using YAML parsing and shows how to tie environment mapping to PR gates.

## Key Concepts

- Kubernetes namespaces
- Helm charts values.yaml
- YAML parsing with yq
- GitHub Actions gate
- Environment-specific deployments

## Code Example

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
ENV="${ENV:-dev}"
for f in manifests/**/*.yaml; do
  NS=$(yq e '.metadata.namespace // ""' "$f")
  if [[ -z "$NS" || "$NS" != "$ENV" ]]; then
    echo "Namespace mismatch: $f -> '$NS' (expected '$ENV')"
    exit 1
  fi
done
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to implement a basic software supply chain gate: SBOM generation and vulnerability scanning integrated into CI, with clear pass/fail criteria.

## Key Concepts

- SBOM generation with Syft
- Vulnerability scanning with Trivy
- GitHub Actions workflow basics
- Exit-code driven gates and report interpretation

## Code Example

```yaml
name: SBOM and vulnerability gate
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t service:latest .
      - name: Generate SBOM
        uses: anchore/syft-action@v0
        with:
          image: service:latest
      - name: Trivy scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0
        with:
          image: service:latest
          severity: HIGH,CRITICAL
          format: table
          exit-code: 1
```

```dockerfile
# Failing Dockerfile (vulnerable)
FROM debian:stretch-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
```

```dockerfile
# Passing Dockerfile (secure, updated base)
FROM debian:bullseye-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adjust thresholds for different environments?
- How would you add caching and parallel scans to speed up CI?
